blocks.html:
You quote the policy to a client, and they read it back to you a week later — from their own notes. The version you used came from a document in a Teams channel. It was the working draft. The approved version, on the Hub, said something slightly different in the paragraph that mattered.

Nothing about the search felt risky. You found a document with the right name, in a place colleagues use, and it answered the question. What it couldn't tell you was whether it was the version.

That's the difference this lesson is about: a channel is where work is argued out, and the Hub is where the answer is kept.

By the end of this lesson you'll be able to:

  1. Tell which of the two places a document belongs in, and know which one to trust when they disagree.
  2. Find the approved version of a policy, standard or template, and check the one you've been using.
  3. Contribute what you learn — in the right channel, in a form someone else can use.

About 15 minutes. Keep the Hub open in another tab — you'll be checking a real document against it.

One question, two places

“What's our current policy on this?” Both of these will produce an answer today. Only one survives being checked.

Found in a Teams channelFound on the Hub
What it isA version someone was working on, possibly the final one, possibly not.The approved version, kept in one place.
Who can change itAnyone in the channel, at any time, usually without telling you.Administrators only, so what you read stays read.
Six months laterTwo or three copies, and no way to tell which one was adopted.The same document, still current, or replaced by a newer approved one.
When a client asks you to prove itYou can't say where it came from or whether it was approved.You can send the link.

So the working rule: if you're quoting it to a client or relying on it as a standard, it has to come from the Hub. If there's no approved version there yet, that's a gap worth reporting — not a reason to use the draft.

What the Hub is for

The Hub holds information that is finished, rarely changed, and useful beyond one team: oneaccord.sharepoint.com/sites/WelcomeOneAccord

  • Official policies and procedures — compliance documents and operational procedures.
  • Standards and reference guides — branding standards, report templates, technical specifications.
  • Sales and marketing resources — final, approved, client-facing documents.
  • Archive — historical, non-client material kept but no longer edited.

Your role on the Hub is to read, search and reference. You won't post or edit there. If something should be added or corrected, raise it with Jesse or Abby.

SharePoint, two ways. The Files tab behind a Teams channel is SharePoint too — it's the collaborative space from Lesson 4. The Hub is a separate site with a different job. Same technology, opposite rules: one is where work happens, the other is where the answer lives.

Hub or channel?

You need to…Go toBecause
Look up final, approved informationThe HubRead-only, administrator-managed, the current approved version
Draft, edit or argue about a documentThe Teams channel's Files tabThe team works on it together there

The company-wide team: Wins, Lessons, Resources, Events

This is the team that crosses departments — culture, knowledge sharing, questions that don't belong to one project. The channels are open and lightly used, which means your participation is most of what makes them valuable. In Teams each channel name carries a small icon in front of it; the names in this table are the words to search for.

ChannelUse it forHow to contribute
#WinsCelebrating, lightlyReact (🎉, ❤️) and reply briefly. For a win you want recognised at the all-team meeting, also post a Ninety.io Headline (Lesson 6).
#Shared LessonsWhat a finished project taught you: what worked, what to avoidNew post with a specific subject line, then invite discussion in replies
#ResourcesArticles, notes from events, material that could help the wider teamNew post with a clear subject; keep discussion in replies
#EventsTraining, gatherings, internal deadlinesPost it here, check it regularly, and react to confirm you saw it

Lesson 3's etiquette matters more here, not less: reply in the thread, and reserve @Team for something genuinely relevant to every person in the company.

Where a lesson becomes a standard. #Shared Lessons is where you say what you learned. The Hub is where it becomes the approved way to do something, if it's good enough and general enough to be one — and that move goes through Jesse or Abby. Posting in #Shared Lessons and assuming it's now policy is how a channel draft ends up being quoted to a client.

blocks.prompt: You need the approved, current version of a company policy. Where do you look?
options: A private chat with a colleague
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. The Hub is the single source of truth for approved documents.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: The Hub holds the approved version. A chat or your inbox gives you someone's copy of it.

blocks.prompt: You find an outdated document on the Hub. What do you do?
options: Raise it with Jesse or Abby so it can be corrected
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The Hub is read-only for staff, so corrections go through Jesse or Abby.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: You can't edit the Hub. Raise it with Jesse or Abby — and until it's fixed, don't quote the old version.

blocks.prompt: Your team is revising a document together this week. Where does it live?
options: In the Teams channel's Files tab
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Active editing happens in the channel; the Hub is for what's finished.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A document being worked on lives in the channel's Files tab. The Hub only holds approved versions.

blocks.prompt: You read an article that would help people well beyond your project. Where does it go?
options: A new post in #Resources with a clear subject line
A private chat to the people you think need it
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. #Resources is for exactly this, and a clear subject line is what makes it findable later.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Firm-wide knowledge sharing goes in #Resources. A chat helps the three people you picked and nobody after them.

blocks.promptHtml:
You're preparing a proposal and need the firm's current approved wording for a contractual clause. You find three versions:

  • One in the project channel's Files tab, edited three weeks ago by a colleague.
  • One on the Hub, last updated last year.
  • One attached to an email from a former colleague, six months old.

None of them agree. What do you do — and what do you do about the fact that they disagree?
rubric: Uses the Hub version as the approved one, and checks the others against it rather than choosing the newest or the nearest
Recognises that the channel copy and the emailed copy aren't authoritative, whatever their dates
Escalates the discrepancy — raises it with Jesse or Abby so the Hub version is confirmed or corrected — rather than deciding alone
Keeps the proposal from going out on an unverified clause until the approved wording is confirmed
Names the underlying cause: an approved document being copied, edited and emailed around instead of referenced where it lives
blocks.coachContext: The Hub holds approved, administrator-managed versions and is the reference for anything quoted or relied on. A document in a channel or an email attachment may be newer, older or unauthorised; recency is not authority. When versions disagree the learner should use the Hub version, raise the discrepancy with Jesse or Abby so the approved version is confirmed or corrected, and keep the client-facing document from going out on unverified wording. The cause is copying an approved document into channels and inboxes instead of linking to where it lives. No prices.

blocks.promptHtml:
Different conditions: this time you're the source.

You finished an engagement and found a way of running the kickoff meeting that worked much better than the usual approach. Two colleagues on other projects have already asked you to send them “whatever you used.” One of them says the firm should make it the standard.

Where does it go, in what order, and what do you deliberately not do?
rubric: Shares it in #Shared Lessons with a specific subject line, as a post others can discuss and add to, rather than sending files to two people
Points people at the post instead of attaching copies, so the material lives in one place and improves as people comment
Raises the idea of making it a standard with Jesse or Abby rather than declaring it the new standard
Waits for the approved version to reach the Hub before treating it as the firm's way of doing it
Names the sequencing: share and discuss first, approve second, publish to the Hub third
blocks.coachContext: A reusable lesson or method is shared in #Shared Lessons as a post with a specific subject, so it can be discussed and improved; sending copies to individuals produces scattered versions. Nothing is a firm standard until it's approved and on the Hub, and Hub changes go through Jesse or Abby. The order is: share and discuss, then approve, then publish to the Hub. The learner should not announce a new standard on their own authority.

blocks.prompt: A teammate posts a better way of doing something in #Shared Lessons, and it's genuinely good. Is it now the firm's standard?
options: Yes, if enough people react to it
Yes, because #Shared Lessons is the firm-wide channel
Only once it's approved and on the Hub
Only if a Managing Principal replies to the post
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. #Shared Lessons starts the conversation; the Hub is where an approved standard lives.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A good post is a proposal, not a standard. It becomes one when it's approved and published on the Hub.

blocks.label: In the Hub
blocks.instructions:
Open the OneAccord Hub and check something you actually use:
  • Find the approved version of a policy, standard or template you rely on — the one you'd quote to a client.
  • Compare it with what you've been using. Same version, or a copy that's drifted?
  • Note one thing. If they differ, raise it with Jesse or Abby. If they match, note where the approved version lives so you go there next time instead of searching a channel.

Also find where the sales and marketing resources sit. That's the folder people ask about most.

criteria: The takeaway separates approved reference from working collaboration, rather than describing the Hub as 'where documents are'
The answer on the disagreement uses the Hub version and escalates — it does not pick the newest or decide alone
The contribution path names #Shared Lessons first, then approval through Jesse or Abby, then the Hub

coachPersona: You are an experienced OneAccord team member coaching a new colleague through the OneAccord Digital Standard, which covers Outlook, Microsoft Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint (the OneAccord Hub) and Ninety.io. The firm's standard: Outlook email is for external parties and anything needing a formal record; Teams channel posts are the default for internal group work and day-to-day decisions; Teams private chat is for quick questions between one or two people; OneDrive is your own workbench for drafts and never the local hard drive; once a group is collaborating, files live in the Teams channel's Files tab. The OneAccord Hub is the SharePoint reference site for finished, approved information — read-only for staff, and changes to it go through Jesse or Abby. The company-wide Wins, Lessons, Resources team in Teams is where knowledge is shared and discussed before anything is approved. Ninety.io Headlines are for items the whole firm should see at the all-team meeting. Coach judgment: which of the two places a piece of information belongs in, and why. No prices quoted. OneAccord's values are truth, compassion and service.
